Certainly as this season unfolds we are testing some of the newer provision. These discussions start very early and we try to take lessons from the field, if you will, immediately to inform the type of changes we want to make in the next Farm Bill reauthorization. The commodity prices being low is still a challenge to many.

Several weeks ago, we talked with Colin Peterson, the ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, and he shared his frustration with the dairy program of the Farm Bill and Most recently, he's been quoted of saying that if the farm economy gets worse, then he'll be up for discussion of riding a new farm bill early or coming to the aid of producers. Right now, the dairy margin program is not protecting our farmers. And we're seeing a number of problems, including that it isn't kicking in soon enough. So there's a lot of talk in the dairy industry right now about how we can update the dairy program to better serve this sector. And I will tell you, I agree with Colin Peterson. It is an important conversation that we're having on the ground in Wisconsin, and I'm gathering input from across the industry, producers as well as processors. I think that whether it is action that we take now that complements fixing the dairy margin program. And so if Colin Peterson has suggested that we go back to the drawing board immediately and pass something early out of the reauthorization cycle, I am very open to hearing that. I want to know sort of what direction we're going in. But right now I can just sort of emphatically agree that the new dairy margin program is not protecting our dairy farmers.

turn_text: What's happening in Canada with regard to their pricing? Some might say, well, this is another reason not to have trade agreements because this is what happens. And frankly, we're seeing trade as a major issue in other parts of the world. That said, my fight on behalf of all the constituents that I represent is to ensure that those current trade agreements that are in existence are upheld to protect our dairy producers among others. So as we're looking at Canada, we're talking about do these new pricing policies, do they comply and comport with already existing agreements between our two nations, whether that's NAFTA or others? Looking forward to pending trade agreements, both the TPP and the currently, it's in the process of being negotiated transatlantic treaty and investment partnerships, otherwise known as TTIP. You know, as a senator, I weigh the impact of the trade deal on all of the state's diverse economic interests. And for TPP, I have concluded that they fall well short of delivering the shared prosperity that we want to see for all Wisconsin's workers, whether those be agricultural or manufacturing workers. There is one particular issue I want to tease out with regard to TTIP. the one that's still being negotiated, that has a pretty disproportionate impact on our state given its dairy industry and other things that are not necessarily unique to Wisconsin, but special about Wisconsin. And that is the issue of geographic indicators. In the negotiations, the European Union has been sticking hard to a view that they should be able to have exclusive use of certain names that we commonly know for cheeses, for beers, for brats. And if you think about Wisconsin, you often think about cheesebear and brats. We can say it sort of lightheartedly, but we have had literally generations of craft and master cheesemakers, sausage manufacturers, and craft beer industry participants who use names that would be banned or prohibited in their youth by the European Union if we don't succeed in getting rid of this particular provision in that future trade deal. And my dairy industry has made it very clear that this is a huge priority and vital to our state's economy and frankly our state's heritage.
